title: Sita as a character !
content:
As I am reading the story of Sita through the lens of Chitra Banerjee, I am deeply in love with Sita. From the childhood, I was always attracted to the "Mahabharata" more than the "Ramayana". It may be due to the environment in which I was grown up. Its in our tradition to utter "Krishna" in everything. So, by the time I can understand anything about God, spirituality and religion, I always considered 'Krishna' to be the one God. This has not changed even after I have grown up. Now, I know both are the incarnation of the same God, but yet when I have to visualise God, its always "Krishna". One more thing, a far as I can remember, I have always questioned about Ram abandoning "Sita" at the end, even in my childhood. When I was reading and trying to recollect how and what ideas about Sita I hold form my childhood, I am recalling the stories my maternal grandmother told us. She was a great storyteller, I can still remember those nights, she used to tell stories to us. Me, ba, Aaijoni and Pallab sitting around her, demanding her to tell the same stories again and again. There is an Assamese novel "Bideh Nandini" (I thing I have remembered it correctly), by Dr. Malini. And it was featured in the Sunday magazine "Purbachal" by "amar axom" as a serial (I do not know the word for it, if it has any).  Aaita used to keep waiting to read it, once she read, when she meet us she will then tell the story in her own way. And she used to give it a new version (that I have imagined, because I have never read that novel, but the interpretations were so coded to Aaita herself that I now think it may be so) and tell it. She has mostly told the stories after Sita has been kidnapped by Ravana, and she was kept in the cage. I remember how Aaita would feel pity for Sita, how sometimes telling the story she will almost break out crying. And I somehow developed an affection for Sita. At the end when Ram rescued Sita and then questioned her purity, I was angry and the little mind of mine would rebel to accept Ram as a God. And I was even more angry at Ram when I have learnt the fate of Sita, the story about "fat mela boxumati patale lukao". I remember me debating about Ram being a God with my grandmother and grandfather. Though I have this sweet corner, I always looked upto Krishna, Arjun and Draupadi, never to Ram and Sita. Now, this book of Chitra Banerjee has make me feel deeply about Ram and Sita. As I am still to reach the part with Ravana in this book, I am touched by the love between Sita and Ram. How wonderful of a woman Sita is! How beautifully she embraces the flaws of Ram. Sometimes reading the book I question myself, shouldn't I learn this from my beloved character! I definitely should, and I would try my best. 


---> She Donkey

content:

title: Finally, I finished
content:
Yesterday night I finished the Days at the Morisaki Bookshop. It is indeed a small novel. As I had a huge gap in between, it took me almost one and a half months to complete it. But, I finished it, it is indeed a little achievement for me, who was struggling to read. As I finished the book and was thinking about it, I discovered one thing. At the beginning of the book, it completely got me. I was obsessed with the book town and the morisaki bookstore itself. And then how Takako found a new love, her love for reading books. The smell of the coffee of saveur and the comforting feeling of reading a novel in a coffee shop. These are all things a book lover will definitely love. Apart from that, what specifically about the story and the protagonists life I was deeply touched with! I couldn’t think of many. The author ( Satoshi Yagisawa) has kept the story simple, the protagonist Takako doesnot posses any extraordinary characteristics (like many fictional characters does). Nothing fancy happens in her life. Most of the incidents described in the novel can pretty usually happen to any one of us, and we witness it with many of our friends and acquaintances. But the beauty is, the simplicity has made it a cozy read. A cute little novel to read. But it’s not a kind that has a impact in your life, or the kind you can’t help but think about even after you finish it. I overall like the book, it was a good read but not something I would love to go back again. At the beginning I thought and expected it, but as the story progresses, I somehow keep losing that soul connection. 


—-She Donkey

content:
with what fear i initially had with the next chapter on Urvashi Butalia's book, it turns out that although the having the fear part is justified, but several aspects are there in reality for which the chapter does not feature much horrific narration and aspects than it does in the previouos chapters, women and horror. the core reason is simple, during the partition they were children and during childhood, it's often not their own view but the surroudings or whomever they were guarded with. i could not think about this beforehand. i was mostly thinking on the horrific description the book will contain, there are definitely. but the description and the emotion it should contain (similar to the previous) is not the same. on the other hand, the lot many children were lost and they are not easily recognizable now, where are they, who have they become -  because many of them were adopted later on, no connection with their own family, many had to go to the orphange, and apparently the girl child was taken for some other 'services'. it features an interview of a person who was child and narrate his story how he somehow could live his life amidst all the killings. when it was the time, and the male members were thinking of preserving the honor of the family and the ease to flee away to a safe place, the women, children, the older ones who can't move easily, were 'martyred'. however this mentioned child was saved, becasue he requested his uncle not to slit through his neck and promised he won't be a problem in the entire process of fleeing away. one sentence that Urvashi butalia also highlighted from his interview, he said the situation was like that the rich go to rich for help and the poor go to the poor, but it was not the default scenario before parition. Earlier even the poor went to the rich and was helped. 

the chapter has a lot of questions (for which i appreciate the author Urvashi Butalia) which shows the careful research methodology she has considered. actually those are not questions, actually the precautionary considerations one must make before concluding anything. this chapter thus has helped my thought proceess horizon to grow a bit larger and teach to be careful when approaching to any topic or any process or on anyting.

title: the logic of art
content:
it is finally one science based book I am taking out to read, the gene machine by Venki Ramakrishnan. i heard about it but I am a poor student when it comes to biology. since i left biology after class X, a lot of knowledge gap, numerous misconception and a handful of embarassment sessions for not knowing simple biology knowledge made me take the decision, only knowing some physics is not enough. that is what i have been feeling several times ago, i even tried to read the class XI, XII biology in my early phd days. however, the surge did not continue for long but the new curiosity i felt was enough to get the motivation consistently. i preassumed the book to be full of a lot of biology i maynot be able to understand, however, turns out it is not. the initial chapters actually remind me of Dr. Rubul Maut's book, although this book is not a motivational one. it features the journey of V Ramakrishnan how he finally deciphers one of the most complex topics in human race, the secrets of ribosome. the most fascinating thing is, he was a physicist. the another interesting thing is, he went up to join phd at the age of 19 to US, and secured one when he was 23. although I was not aware of him, i instantly got one idea, the man who is writing this book, is not one that we usually come to meet in our day-to-day life. 

i have come up to know many intertesting 'trivia' such as Bragg's laws Bragg was the son of a father, who himself was a renowned professor and when Bragg- the son, discoverd Bragg's law, he thought one day his father will steal the credit of this when they wrote a joint article. i could not think of this, the kind of relationship people might have when it comes to intellectual property. V, Ramakrishnan, when he went for phd, he was setup to meet a lady, who happend to be divorcee, and later they got married and he wrote , 'this way i become a stepfather of a daughter and i had to become responsible at the age 23' (not that similar, but the idea is this).. in one of the chapters, he wrote about one professor I think Berlin (the name is berline or something that sort, it started w B as far as I remember) .. who happens to have a lot of good relationship with different ladies simultaneously. venky wrote that even those ladies know about him yet they were all in good terms w him. this kind of description i also found in the autobiography of Dr. Kulendu Pathak. probably when people talk about scientists, it is mostly the science they care, but the art of scientists life is only found in such books. 

i spent some time in chapter 3 where he was describing the biology, for example, the gene, the dna, the mRna, protein structure, amino acid, - all these were to get into the core, the ribosome. although i tried to understand it, yet i know there is still some fog remained, hopefull will be able to understand it as the book progress. the following chapter was really good coz he wrote about how physics comes to handy for molecular biology and many of the physics concepts is written there as problem-then solution kind, which often is not found in typical textbooks - the reason which many of the students like me have to struggle understanding the gist of a new physical concepts. 

although the book is of similar length to Anita Desais novel, i will read it slow.

title: looking out to the sea
content:
it was really not planned, but I have finished reading a novel, the village by the sea by Anita Desai. I did not know such book exist untill i picked the copy and bought it instantly from a local book store which I hardly do now-a-days, mostly because the price is lowered if I buy it from online market, and also because the soft copy can be accessed in the internet-the practice, although, is not morally correct if you are having it for free. this is the first time i have met Anita Desai, curious enough, i read about her in the book itself. the book has it written award winning novel, however, which award they did not mention. i like the cover art and in the back cover the publisher has written 2-3 lines on what the book is going to be about. i understood Desai is actually a big shot and from the acknowledgement part, i readily understood she wrote one book just to pay honor to her days in a village by a sea near bombay. how writeous you have to be that you complete writing a book to let the world know what you felt about the time you really enjoy being.. I don't know but i admire it a lot. 

the book is about a family living in the coast and their stories revolving in the village. it's a sweet story, like similar template kind we actually come across on a day-to-day basis, and comes into our notice only when somebody presented it before us in an unique way. Desai is successful in that entirely (however I still believe that she didnot write it to impress the reader,  and i can not judge her on that basis). the book is divided into 12 or 13 chapters, with each chpater has its own subsections separated inside. Probably i also picked up the book because i am having a curiosity grown inside to know the local stories of indian villages more and through the lens of indian english writers. yes, definitely i will pick a book if it has a story based on a remote village next, to know them, to know their unique enviroment yet similar humanly feeling. 

the speed of the book is steady, average and it gets you going. its around 250 page long novel. i could guess the positive ending of the story (which definitely had to be) and so sometimes I thought i would go slow on the book (means I would end it later, read one chapter a day). I terminated this plan. 

having praised the language of the book, i also noticed one thing- while i was reading everything about the nearby village of the sea and everything, i did not get enough motivation to see the village, probably because Desai focused more on the description of the events. it does feature some description for sure, however, many times i felt it like a movie with not so accurate color grading. Although there is 5-6 percentage chance that I may miss the beauty because i read it fast. however, this point can be defied too as the descritpion of coconut tree, sea side and all I could vividly picturised, however there still lacks some extra elements that was required for me to have gained enough excitement to go see the actual place. 

I just thought and maybe figured it out, maybe-- maybe, the thing about the extra motivation may come from my inner expectations too. While I 'watched' the movie kambalangi nights, i instantly wanted to go that village. probably while I was reading this book, i craved a similar picturisation in my mind. because i already had this so itched in my mind, i may have missed some amount of beauty of the Thul village from this novel or i completely fail to load this in my imagination thouroughly or replace it. this  however i think is normal because that was a movie, and this is a book. 

i will definitely recommend the book. some english i don't know, was used in a manner i am not familiar with or i previously thought was grammatically incorrect. for example, when somebody possess something and we ask if they posses it, we ask, 'do you have this thing?' in the book, Desai writes, 'have you this thing?' - i could not be sure about it why it is written that way. i want to correct me in this if I am not learnt this way (too lazy to google search it). I am sure that was not used colloquially.

I want to thank Desai for the beautiful creation and let the reader know how beautiful small stories can be!.

title: Oh Preeti !
content:
I have not read for a long time. I went home and got busy with some stuff that I couldn't even read a single page ( this may be an excuse), and now I have to build the habit from scratch. But I watched the series "Musafir Cafe" on netflix. One of my friend recommended me to watch, and I started watching without any expectations. As I started watching, it got me in many ways. It starred Vikrant Messi, that's definitely an USP for me. Another was the Musafir Cafe itself. I had (maybe I still have) a dream of opening my own cafe; a cafe where artist can come, jam, talk, I want to provide the atmosphere of a good adda point for the artists in my cute little cafe. And one of my visualization is to have a lots of books in the walls of the cafe. The concept of "musafir cafe" was very different, but the very idea that the protagonist who used to be a software engineer has a dream of opening his own cafe hit me differently. And then Preeti's dream of opening an Artist Residency; somehow my dream is a mixture of the dreams of Preeti and  Chander. And Preeti ! I could relate to her in so many ways. In my scenes I could exactly feel Preeti. It feels like, to some context I am living the life of Preeti. Is love really supposed to be that bittersweet !  Its a beautiful love story, I cannot blame any of the protagonist for what they are doing and its consequences. Everyone is right at their own place. But then, the ending !! I hope the script writer could have been little more generous towards Preeti.  I know its an open ending, one can assume anything. We even don't know if season 2 comes, what will it serve on the plate. But for people like me, waiting to see Preeti happy, to see Preeti get what she deserves, this ending can be little unsettling !

This series left me with one question, why in love those who choose themselves over their loved one's are always the central character? Why not those who sacrifice themselves for their love?

I am editing this post, because everyone reading it may think I am insensitive towards Sudha. No, I am not. I totally understand Sudha. She is an incredible woman. I love how she support Chander, how she uplift Chander. Even when he fails to believe in himself, she believes in him and she implant that believe in him. That's why I wrote before that I have to say everyone is right at their own position. Maybe if I wouldn't feel the personal connection to Preeti, I would have love Sudha more. She may not be the textbook definition of  a good lover/ woman, but she is pure. Her love is pure. The colours, love and energy she bring to Chander's life is what make Chander what he is today. But at the same time, there is Preeti, who has pour her everything in love. I could not but being little selfish towards her. 


---> She Donkey

title: the title theory
content:
I am a bit skeptical with my entry today as I am writing using my laptop and I have to press it really hard because the keys are malfunctioned. nonetheless keeping my enthusiasm in check, I am putting my thoughts here as it is boiling since i read the next story of heart lamp and this time it is the star of the book, 'heart lamp'. usually i have this idea in my mind, i have seen older short story books where they are named as 'a story name and other selected story name'. and that story which is featured in the title is usually the best one (from authors perspective and readers as well; in very rare cases it is wrong). So, by default, i preassumed the story has to be the best among all. also I saw some social media story where people has widely appreciated banu for the book and the idea she conveys through it. so, the expectation naturally got high. 

i started the story. it has been 3-4 days i didnot touch it because of an exam. however when i again picked it up, immediately i was taken to the familiar environment banu creates and it didnot feel foreign. i felt like going back to a familiar place once felt very home. somehow i felt this story has a velocity (not speed) that makes it standout. although i could guess the direction, the speed is Banu's writing superiority than any other regular writer. 

towards the ending, i just couldnot think anything else, but just surrendering myself to banu's pen, and follow wherever she wants to takes us to. probably i read it in one short breath (towards the end). i felt magic. she writes magic. the story was a magic (it is a magic). after I end it, i feel so refreshed and felt like i should share it, sometimes we feel this kinda rush to tell somebody when we come to know juicy gossips. although gossip is not fitting here, but the rush inside the body was there. 

while I praise the story for the magic she paints there, the ending lines i still seek something more (probably because the ending lines of previous stories were more solid or maybe i was too drawn away). this is a very personal view. maybe due to the hormonal rush, i couldnot pay that much of an attention that was desired and required. whatever it is, banu is another author coz of whom I will further carry this belief that usually it is the best story that gets featured in the title of a short story collection. 


-- Male Donkey

title: can you predict a story !
content:
When you read a book (or even watch a movie), the curiosity in you always devote some of your imagination to predict what is going to happen later, how the story will take turn. There is a joy in being correct. You feel like a winner. But, sometimes the writer proves you to be completely wrong. You predict something the story take a complete different turn. In that case, sometimes you are disappointed with the story, and in other times you can do nothing but falling in love with the story even more. For me (and I guess for everyone), the later makes your reading even more interesting. And it is the power of the creativity the writers use (anyway every person will have a different way of imagination). I am experiencing exactly that with this book, "Days at the Morisaki BookShop". The story is not very unpredictable, like completely not aligning with what I have imagined it to be. But the unexpected turns that the life of uncle Satoru and Takako ( I finally remember her name) is taking is literally keeping me hooked to the book. I am, in my imagination roaming around the streets of Jimbocho, I am taking a sip of coffee at 'Saveur' enjoying my evening with that soft piano music and the fresh aroma of coffee with a secondhand ( and maybe new) book in my hand. One thing I always see in the movies and also read in books that people go to coffee shops with books, they sat alone, read their book and enjoy coffee. I very much romaticize that thing. I doubt if there will be any place in  here where I can do the same without the fear of being judged.  Some people read everywhere, in cafes, in trains,  in flight, even in buses. I find those people very magnanimous. Instead of scrolling through our phones, cannot we make this our new normal !

One more thing I want to write for today. As I previously mentioned, my liking for uncle Satoru's character is growing with every chapter I read. Lately, I found out that the bond between him and his wife is less like a married couple and more like old friends. That's exactly resonate with what I personally want from my partner. And so, my love for uncle Satoru and Momoko has found yet another reason to grow.

title: there is really a booktown !
content:
So, that's the thing. I kind of fall in love with the Morisaki Bookshop ( I am kind of obsessed). Today I googled about that place to see if it's a real place. Not exactly though, there is probably no Morisaki Bookshop but the neighbourhood Jimbocho is real. It's a book town in Tokyo, and really the largest used-book neighbourhood in the world, with small cafes and restaurants. Okay, now I have another place in the long bucket list of places I want to visit in my life (I have so many places that I have fallen in love with from books, videos, movies even from newspaper; and it is my dream that I will visit those places once in my lifetime). This is the beauty of reading, you can fall in love with places and people even without seeing them. How beautifully the authors have to panned it down so that you can feel it while reading the words. And I personally think you can feel it more deeply when you read than when you see it in a video or something (it is possible that this may vary from person to person). One reason why I feel like this maybe because my first connection with the outside world was through books and newspapers. But anyway, I am bragging so much about just the book neighbourhood that one may start thinking that the story of the book is all about that bookshop only. And I a falling in love just romanticizing about the book town. But there is something fresh about the story, the story is I guess mainly about starting a new journey and discovering oneself. The protagonist ( I am having a hard time remembering her name, I remember Hideaki, Tomo, uncle Satoru but could not remember her, yesterday I looked at her name while writing today I am not doing it so that I can get a push to remember it), was in the Morisaki bookshop after she left both her job and her boyfriend. She is discovering this new life in Jimbocho and is loving it, which she never  thought she would. And a big part of it is uncle Satoru, the owner of the Morisaki Bookshop. 

As I am reading through the book, my liking for uncle Satoru's character is growing with every chapter. He is man who loved doing so many things in his youth with so many aspirations; and then he settled at the secondhand bookshop his family has owned for generations. There was a dialogue from him where he say that after roaming all around the world, when he finally came back to that bookshop then he realised that no matter where he is or with whom, but if he could be honest with himself, then that was where he belonged ( this is not the exact dialogue but it is what he meant). This touches my heart and I also think if we cannot be totally honest with ourselves we can never be really happy.

title: algorithm everywhere
content:
Today I picked up a new book to read “The days at the morisaki bookshop”. I have bought this book long back. Maybe at the beginning of 2025. Once I even picked up the book to read it, but somehow I never did. I always had a fascination about books and bookstores. This book was kind of very famous in somewhere around 2024. She/he ( although I mainly assume the main character to be a girl) will meet another visitor and will fall in love ( I have an absurd habit of assuming things a priori, its a reflection of the same). But, it’s not certainly like that, the protagonist is someone who is kind of working in the morisaki bookshop. The most beautiful thing I can imagine while reading this book is the location of the morisaki bookshop. It is located in a place which according to the book used to be the largest destination for secondhand books. Rows and rows of bookstores in both side of the road, and some little cafes and bars in between. It’s nothing like a heaven for someone who likes books ( I would definitely love to live in such a neighbourhood). I am very interested to know how the story takes turn and how the morisaki bookshop will change Takako’s life. 

One more interesting thing that caught my mind while reading was that, the protagonist Takako is falling in love with reading books just in the story. From being a girl who sleeps all the extra tome she got, she built the habit of reading of books ( she literally read from night till morning to finish a book that single night. that was some tale of very long past for me). That’s exactly what we are trying to do here. Nowadays, all the social media platforms saw us things we think about, talk about. We see contents very relatable to what’s happening in our life. It’s interesting that the book I pick up to read also happens to do the same thing (algorithm worked here to, lol).

title: hope is a good thing, but not from others.
content:
i did read the partition related book remnants of separation - through material memory by Malhotra.  Anchal Malhotra now I remember. A book I accidently loved (accidently because I was never that aware of partition before - this is also sad at the same time). I knew that there were riots and many other incidents took place, but the atrocities I could never feel (again, because I didnot know much about it). I only came to know about it through the Malhotra book. I was driven by the book, the stories it has, and the way each stories is presented, narrated. Each story was unique and had a purpose to stay in that book. From almost every angle and perspective, the book is filled with stories with utmost care. 

however, i am not going to illustrate about the Malhotra book. The new book I am writing here is the the other side of silence. now I really forgot the authors name, she is lady though. I only remember one of her maternal uncle's name, ranamama, (i hope i am correct in this). I remember this because the book is also dedicated to him. I have read the acknowledgement section and the first chapter. The way she acknowledges people gives me the feel that it is actually a PhD level research outcome, not a casual one. Malhotra;s book is also similar, they did a lot of research, work, visits, capturing recording - and this is why that makes it what it is - an outstanding piece of art. I will look at the authors name. Her name is Urvashi Butalia. 

Butalia expresses gratititude to so many people, profressionally and personal one as well. She kept on mentioning about people who gave her casual and not-so-casual feedback (which I actually liked). Gradually I got the idea the book is indeed going to be a serious one. Then I read the first chapter,'the beggining'.  I thought that chapter is some kind of what the book will be about, (yes definitely it is), but there she is using that chapter as an broad introcution to why she is doing the book, why this kind of work she decided to pubclish the book and how was the things that was bothering her during the preparations. actually this is the chapter that descibes how her book is actually different from rest of the partition related book. Even I was thinking that if this book also says about partition, is not it going to be almost similar to the Malhotra's one? 

however, this is only in my mind and neither Butalia, nor Malhotra is competing with each other. In addition, I think Butalia's book is published before Malhotra. After reading the first chapter, I understood the core difference will be in the methodology. Definitely, Malhotra was clear that her book will be based on the material memory, and there was no such mention in Butalia. then why I was thinking about the similarity? Because I was thinking that ultimately it's about the parition incident only, by any means. 

And then I found one paragraph in Butalia's book. She said while they were interviewing, people did not want to talk about it at the first instant. why? because that was so brutal, so brutal that they didnot want to talk about it. and that is where things become different and more interesting. what is there that people wants to avoid talking about it or don't want to recall about it? can we capture that emotion? can we get it out from them so that they feel "..." a word I learnt yesternight from the book, now I forgot. the word means 'a kind of feel one feels when the weight lifts off the shoulder'..

and in the process, Urvashi Butalia said it was actually a process she thought she would not be able to continue because the interviewing of that intense talks were a bit harsh for her sometimes (i mean she could not imagine such kind of brutality really exist?).

I will look forward and hope the book won't disappoint me.


-- Male Donkey

title: Sister of my Heart
content:
Yesterday night I finished reading the book "Sister of my Heart" by Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni. It took me more than four months to read this book. Not like I am not liking the book or something. I was loving it from the beginning. Although I took four months to finish it, I still consider it as an achievement. My brain is rotted to a level that I start books, I find it interesting, I read it for few days, then I leave it and completely forget about it. Then I pick up a new book after one or two months. Then the cycle repeats. This writing about what we learn from reading can be  a way to break this cycle. I am hopeful and enthusiastic about it. Anyway, the book, Chitra Banerjee has written the stories of two sisters; two sisters connected by souls. Two sisters brought up in a household with only women. Although the story was set up in late 80s, I could still relate. I myself is grown up with my sister, in our childhood we also shared a similar kind of bond like Anju and Sudha (maybe we are no longer the sisters of our hearts like Anju and Sudha are till the end of the story). The big dreams that Anju had from her childhood, and the softness of Sudha, remind me of exactly how me and my sister were. The rebellious Anju; Anju inspiring Sudha to be brave, and Sudha supporting Anju in all her adventures. Certainly the circumstances were completely different for me and my sister from that of Anju and Sudha. Chitra Banerjee has picked two women characters, one smart, intelligent, firecious and rebel; and another sweet, beautiful and obedient or I can say the type our society expects a girl/women to be. I am amazed how beautifully she has shaped the women characters. At the beginning of the book, Sudha is the quiet girl, it is expected from her that she is weak, she will behave exactly what the society expects a women to behave. She is portrayed like this, in most of the story she is shown to made sacrifices, for Anju, for their family's reputation.  She is shown to kind of living her life for others (its the exact way most of the women still live their lives, the scenario is changing, that makes me happy sometimes). As the story unfolds her character grows, she became stronger, it give me immense pleasure to see Sudha make the right choice at the end. Sudha choosing herself and her daughter over family's reputation, breaking out from the cage of her in laws house. It give me more happiness to see how the mothers welcome her decision and support her. Women standing for women. I was so happy to see the mothers following a modern lifestyle after that incident. They also broke the cage of their old beliefs and the burden of the fake pride that the society has put on them as the widows of the "chatterjee"s.  

Anju was the one I can mostly relate from the beginning of the book. She was the straightforward, rebellious one from the begging. It hurts me when they had to marry, leaving their dream of higher studies. Then she went to USA. It is strange how leaving so far apart from each other, with all the difficulties/jealousy and everything they had to go though, they still remained each others pillar of support. Initially, I was more drawn towards Anju, as at her childhood part I discovered herself to have the same vibe as mine. But then I fell in love with Sudha's character. Maybe I still resonate more with Anju, but how Sudha evolved was what give me immense joy. Anju had her own battle to fight. She can also be a true inspiration for many women out there. How throughout her life she has shown courage, she is a fighter. I was so sad when she lost "prem" from overworking to save money to support Sudha. How much she loves Sudha that she worked to that extent. I wanted to know more about their life, what will happen in America, can Anju and Sudha begin their boutique. Will Sudha come back and give Ashok another chance. But Chitra banerjee has ended it in a very sweet spot. It made me craving more. Actually, I have a habit, in movies and books, I always keep searching for myself. And when I find a piece of myself, I instantly fall in love. In this book I found it. I am happy that I got it as a gift and read it. 


----> She Donkey

One interesting aspect i liked from the presentation of the story is that, theere is one character who describes some event from his perspective. then from the other perspective, the story unfolds and reader now realises what is actually the case. I like this kind of revealing and self-realisation author compells the reader to make and want to do the same with my own writings too (hopefully someday).  Overall i really liked the story progression and how it ends, mostly because i actually support the social progression the author wish to m ake and describes as an upgrade. 


oh then i also had an idea, in between the reading, i realised probably i did not look at the title (which i usually do or forget in most cases) and then thought let me guess the title or based on the completion of the story i will decide what can be a suitable title. then i thought ah, it's not my story how will i decide and then went up to see the name, and that is how i now remember the title. but then i thought of it, like, why not we can have a book, where the title of the story is written at the end of the story? like the movie names sometime appear at the end of the movie and ends it. i will do this experiment. probably in a book setting it will feel good.

title: New Beginning
content:
Today I read after a long gap. I read just one chapter, maybe 10 pages just. I am still happy, as it is better than reading nothing. I am reading “Sister of my Heart”. Today’s chapter was from Sudha’s lens. Both Anju and Sudha are pregnant. It’s really fascinating to know how the starting of motherhood changes a woman, changes her surroundings. How from the day you become pregnant, the identity of a woman changes. Can she be the woman just the day before, someday in her life! Sometimes I just wonder. As I am growing up, if I try to picture myself in the situation, a fear grows inside me. I can’t imagine further. As in Sudha’s case, the love and care she is getting is kind of suffocating her. That it is compelling her to think if all these love is for the bearer of their grandchildren. Maybe it is. Maybe the extra care is always for the children to come. The mother loses her identity at the very moment she becomes pregnant. The strange thing is the woman itself is happier and anyone else to bring that child to this world. To bring a piece of her to life. 

Maybe now I am writing things I am not supposed to write in this blog. These things are better suited for my diary. Just beginning my journey to writing things about me reading. 


--- She Donkey
